AYRADIA™, sponsored by Virbac AH, Inc., is a flavored liquid formulation administered orally. Clinical studies demonstrated that the drug was over 99% effective at reducing Giardia trophozoites, the active stage of the parasite, in treated dogs. While veterinarians have previously used human-formulated metronidazole in an 'off-label' capacity, this approval provides a product specifically tested for safety and efficacy in dogs and manufactured to quality standards. [1, 2] This new product marks Basepaws as the first company in the pet genetics field to utilize advanced Illumina Next Generation Sequencing (NGS) technology. [1, 2] The test provides dog owners with extensive insights into their pet's health by screening for over 280 genetic markers linked to hereditary conditions, allowing for early detection of disease risks. [2, 3] Additionally, it offers a detailed breakdown of a dog's breed similarity by comparing its genome to a database of over 200 canine breeds and provides information on more than 30 genetic markers that influence physical traits such as coat color, texture, and body size. [1, 2] This technology is a key component of ALRT's animal health division product, the GluCurve Pet CGM, a continuous glucose monitoring system designed to help veterinarians optimize insulin treatment for diabetic pets. Its primary purpose is to slow the development of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) and preserve the effectiveness of these drugs. The strategy outlines three main goals: aligning the use of antimicrobial drugs with stewardship principles, fostering stewardship practices in veterinary settings, and enhancing the monitoring of both antimicrobial resistance and drug use in animals. <5> On September 13, 2023, General Atlantic, a leading global growth equity firm, announced a strategic growth investment in GoodVets Group LLC. [1] The company stated the investment from General Atlantic, which joins existing investor SkyKnight Capital, would accelerate its expansion strategy with new sites planned for New York City, Los Angeles, and Dallas. [1, 4] The ultimate goal is to build the premier national provider of general and urgent veterinary care services. [1, 6] <6> On September 6, 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) granted conditional approval for Fidoquel-CA1 (phenobarbital tablets) to control seizures associated with idiopathic epilepsy in dogs. [1] This condition, which has no known cause, is serious and affects approximately 5% of dogs. [1] While unapproved phenobarbital from the human market has been used in veterinary medicine, Fidoquel-CA1, sponsored by Genus Lifesciences Inc., is the only phenobarbital tablet to receive the FDA's conditional approval for safety, quality manufacturing, and a reasonable expectation of effectiveness. [1, 2] This conditional approval allows the drug to be legally marketed, providing earlier access for a serious condition, while the manufacturer collects the remaining effectiveness data required for full approval. [1, 2] The sponsor has up to five years to obtain full approval, with the initial conditional approval lasting one year and eligible for four annual renewals. [1, 2] Fidoquel-CA1 is the second medication to be conditionally approved for this use, following KBro Vet-CA1 in 2021. [3, 4] <7> On August 21, 2023, Judge Matthew P. Brookman of the U.S. District Court for the Southern District of Indiana granted final approval for a class-action settlement valued at approximately $6.38 million with Midwestern Pet Foods Inc. and its parent company, Nunn Milling Co. The settlement resolves a lawsuit filed by pet owners whose animals either died or became ill after consuming pet food contaminated with high levels of aflatoxin, a toxin from mold, and Salmonella. The issue led to extensive recalls of Sportmix and other pet food brands in 2020 and 2021. The settlement fund was established to compensate consumers for pet injury claims, with provisions for medical expenses and refunds for the purchase of the recalled products.

samples.scenario: Prediction target period: from 2023-11-26 to 2024-02-11. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> In 2023, significant developments in veterinary medicine were announced. The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Bonqat (pregabalin oral solution) on November 17, 2023, as the first pregabalin-containing drug to alleviate anxiety and fear in cats during transportation and veterinary visits. Developed by Orion Corporation, Bonqat is a prescription-only oral solution that showed in studies that 77% of treated cats had improved fear and anxiety levels compared to 46% given a placebo. The product was expected to be commercially available by mid-2024. Separately, on May 2, 2023, Elanco Animal Health announced it had received a conditional license from the U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) for the first-ever monoclonal antibody treatment for canine parvovirus. This single-dose intravenous therapy targets the virus directly and has been shown to decrease mortality. Additionally, the FDA approved new monoclonal antibody treatments for osteoarthritis (OA) pain. On May 5, 2023, Librela (bedinvetmab), a monthly injection for dogs, was approved. This was followed by the approval of Solensia (frunevetmab) for cats, which received its FDA approval on January 13, 2022. Both drugs work by targeting Nerve Growth Factor (NGF) to control pain. <2> On November 17, 2023, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved Bonqat, an oral solution of pregabalin developed to alleviate acute anxiety and fear in cats associated with transportation and veterinary visits. This marked the first time the FDA has approved a drug containing pregabalin for animal use, a significant step in addressing feline stress. Developed by the Finnish pharmaceutical company Orion Corporation, Bonqat is a prescription-only, Schedule V controlled substance due to its potential for human abuse. Clinical trials showed that over 77% of cats given Bonqat demonstrated improvement in fear and anxiety levels during vet exams compared to 46% of those given a placebo. Zoetis holds the exclusive rights to market and distribute the drug in the United States, with an anticipated availability date of mid-2024. <3> TFP Nutrition expanded a voluntary recall on November 16, 2023, due to potential Salmonella contamination, to include all dry dog food, dry cat food, and catfish formulas produced at its Nacogdoches, Texas facility. This action was an expansion of an earlier recall from October 20, 2023. The recall affects multiple brands distributed nationwide and was announced in conjunction with the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA). Salmonella can affect animals that consume the products and poses a risk to humans from handling contaminated pet food. Consumers were advised to stop feeding the recalled products to their pets and dispose of them. <4> Independence Pet Group (IPG), a pet insurance platform operator, secured $55.6 million in a Series C development capital funding round. While the company is sometimes referred to as Chicago-based, other sources identify its headquarters in Raleigh or Scottsdale. The capital was raised from 27 participating investors and is intended to support the growth of the business. The funding follows IPG's acquisition of Felix Cat Insurance in September 2023. <5> TFP Nutrition expanded its October 2023 recall, adding more pet food products due to potential Salmonella contamination. The expansion, announced on November 16, 2023, includes all dry dog food, dry cat food, and catfish formulas produced at the company's Nacogdoches, Texas facility. The initial recall in October was for Retriever All Life Stages Mini Chunk Chicken Recipe Dry Dog Food, but was broadened after a sample tested positive for Salmonella. The recall affects multiple brands distributed nationwide. Health officials warn that humans can contract Salmonella from handling the contaminated pet food, and pets may show symptoms like lethargy, diarrhea, fever, and vomiting. <6> Blue Ridge Beef issued a voluntary recall for a specific lot of its 'Breeders Choice' raw dog food, packaged in 2-pound chubs, due to potential Salmonella contamination. The recall applies to the lot marked with the expiration date '8/2/24' and the UPC number 8 54298 00193 1. The action was taken after the U.S. Food & Drug Administration (FDA) notified the firm on October 27, 2023, that a sample of the product had tested positive for Salmonella.

This was followed by the approval of Senvelgo (velagliflozin), a once-daily liquid oral solution, with its approval announced in 2023. Both drugs are part of a class called SGLT2 inhibitors, which work by causing excess glucose to be excreted in the urine, thus lowering blood sugar levels. These medications are intended for otherwise healthy cats with diabetes mellitus who have not been previously treated with insulin. The introduction of these pill and liquid alternatives has the potential to significantly improve the quality of life for both cats and their owners by simplifying the management of the disease. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> On March 25, 2024, the United States Department of Agriculture (USDA), Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), and Food and Drug Administration (FDA) jointly announced the first-ever confirmed detection of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) H5N1 in dairy cattle. The confirmation came from laboratory samples, including unpasteurized milk and swabs, taken from herds in Texas and Kansas. This event marked a significant cross-species transmission, as it was the first time HPAI had been detected in dairy cattle. The affected cows, primarily older animals, exhibited symptoms such as decreased lactation, low appetite, and fever. Officials believe the virus was likely introduced to the cattle by infected wild birds. While the illness, initially termed a "mystery dairy cow disease," had been observed on farms in Texas, Kansas, and New Mexico in the preceding weeks, the official confirmation and announcement occurred on March 25. Federal agencies stated that the commercial milk supply remained safe due to pasteurization and that the risk to public health was low. <2> The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approved DuOtic on March 15, 2024, as the first treatment specifically for canine ear infections (otitis externa) caused only by susceptible strains of yeast (Malassezia pachydermatis). Developed by Dechra Ltd., this prescription gel is notable for being the first antibiotic-free otic solution approved by the FDA for this condition, marking a significant step in antimicrobial stewardship. The product combines terbinafine, an antifungal, and betamethasone acetate, a steroid for anti-inflammatory purposes. Administered by a veterinary professional in two doses seven days apart, DuOtic dissolves in earwax to provide a long-lasting effect for up to 45 days. <3> The American Veterinary Medical Association's Council on Education (AVMA COE) has scheduled a consultative site visit to Chamberlain University's proposed School of Veterinary Medicine in Stockbridge, Georgia, from August 11-15, 2024. This visit is a crucial step in the accreditation process for the new program. The establishment of the veterinary school aims to expand access to veterinary education and address workforce needs within the profession. <4> An article by Plumb's, a resource for veterinary drug information, published on March 4, 2024, highlighted several innovative treatments expected to be significant in 2024. Key developments included the use of monoclonal antibodies to combat diseases in dogs and cats. Specifically, a monoclonal antibody for canine parvovirus was conditionally licensed by the USDA in 2023. Additionally, gilvetmab, a monoclonal antibody for treating mast cell tumors and melanoma in dogs, was also conditionally licensed. In the area of feline diabetes, two alternatives to insulin were introduced in 2023, including bexagliflozin, the first oral medication approved for treating diabetes in nonhuman animals. These new treatments underscore a period of significant innovation in veterinary medicine, focusing on targeted therapies and more manageable treatment options for pets. <5> By February 2024, reports from veterinary sources indicated that the outbreak of what was termed atypical canine infectious respiratory disease complex (CIRDC), which had caused nationwide concern in late 2023, appeared to be receding. For instance, the Oregon Department of Agriculture, which had received over 200 case reports since August 2023, saw no new reports in January 2024. While the disease, characterized by a persistent cough and sometimes severe pneumonia, had led to speculation about a novel pathogen, the U.S. Department of Agriculture's (USDA) Animal and Plant Health Inspection Service (APHIS) stated there was no evidence to support this conclusion, with testing often identifying common causes of CIRDC. [1] According to the CDC's investigation notice, a total of 63 people have been infected with the outbreak strains of Salmonella (Stanley and Poona) across 22 states. [1] Illnesses started on dates ranging from August 20, 2023, to August 12, 2024. [1] Of the 62 people with available information, 28 (45%) have been hospitalized, with no deaths reported. [1] The median age of those infected is 8 years, with children under 5 being significantly affected. [1] Federal law prohibits the sale and distribution of turtles with shells less than 4 inches long as pets, though they continue to be sold through various outlets. [2, 3] <2> A study published in Nature confirmed multidirectional, interspecies transmission of highly pathogenic avian influenza (H5N1) between mammals on U.S. farms. The research, titled 'Spillover of Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza H5N1 Virus to Dairy Cattle', was first made available as a preprint on May 22, 2024, and was formally published on July 24, 2024. An investigation conducted between February 11 and March 19, 2024, on nine farms across Texas, New Mexico, Kansas, and Ohio provided the foundation for the study. Researchers used whole genome sequencing and epidemiological data to confirm cow-to-cow transmission, as well as transmission from cattle to domestic cats and a raccoon. The study noted that the cats and raccoon likely became infected after consuming raw, unpasteurized milk from sick cows. While the virus has shown the ability to adapt to mammals, researchers noted that whole genome sequencing did not reveal any mutations that would currently lead to enhanced transmissibility in humans. <3> In August 2023, Wyoming reported its first probable human case of leptospirosis since 1983, which occurred in a resident of Laramie County. [3, 8] The patient had occupational exposure to dogs and reported no other risk factors. [4] The case coincided with an outbreak of canine leptospirosis in the same area; 13 canine cases were voluntarily reported by veterinary clinics between August and October 2023. [6] The Wyoming Department of Health (WDH) and the Wyoming Livestock Board initiated a public health investigation to identify infection sources, find additional cases, and recommend control measures. [4, 8] In response, authorities issued a press release to inform the public and healthcare providers and worked with veterinarians to promote vaccination for dogs. [2] Following the public outreach, veterinary clinics in the affected city reported more frequent recommendations for the leptospirosis vaccine and higher compliance from dog owners. [4] <4> The subsequent 98th WVC Annual Conference is scheduled for February 15-18, 2026. [2, 6] <5> Public health officials in Jefferson County, Colorado, confirmed the state's first human case of tularemia in 2024 in a resident of Wheat Ridge. [3, 4, 5] The announcement was made by Jefferson County Public Health (JCPH) and reported by various news outlets. [3, 4] Tularemia, also known as "rabbit fever," is a rare bacterial disease caused by *Francisella tularensis*, which is found in animals like rodents, rabbits, and hares, as well as in insects such as ticks and deer flies. [2, 3] The disease can be transmitted to humans through insect bites, contact with infected animals, consuming contaminated food or water, or inhaling airborne bacteria. [2, 3] While this was a human case, it underscores a health concern for pets, as dogs and cats can also contract the disease through similar means. [2, 7] Symptoms in humans can include fever, skin ulcers, and swollen lymph glands, and if ingested, can cause a sore throat, abdominal pain, and other gastrointestinal issues. [3, 4] In 2023, there were nine reported human cases of tularemia in Colorado. [2, 5] <6> The American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) held its annual convention in Austin, Texas, from June 21-25, 2024. The event drew over 7,300 participants to the Austin Convention Center for five days of education, networking, and entertainment. The convention focused on the latest advancements in veterinary innovation, offering over 650 hours of continuing education through lectures, panels, and workshops. Key topics discussed included Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) H5N1, virtual care (telemedicine), and professional licensure. The event also featured a large exhibit hall with more than 300 exhibitors showcasing new products and services. <7> Viva Raw LLC of Hillsborough, North Carolina, voluntarily recalled five specific raw pet food products from Lot 21244 due to potential contamination with Listeria monocytogenes. The recall was initiated after the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the North Carolina Department of Agriculture (NCDA) discovered the contamination during a facility inspection. While the products in the lot were intended for destruction, some were inadvertently shipped to consumers. The recalled products, which include Viva Turkey for Dogs (Ground and Chunked), Viva Turkey for Cats, Viva Pure Turkey, and Viva Beef & Turkey for Puppies, were distributed directly to consumers in all 50 states and the District of Columbia between May 16 and June 28, 2024. The affected items were sold frozen in 1-pound clear vacuum-sealed packages with no expiration dates. As of the announcement, no illnesses in pets or humans had been reported. Consumers are advised to destroy the product and can contact Viva Raw for a refund. <8> In July 2024, Viva Raw LLC of Hillsborough, North Carolina, announced a voluntary recall for five of its raw pet food products due to potential contamination with *Listeria monocytogenes*. The recall affects Lot #21244, which includes Viva Turkey for Dogs (Ground and Chunked), Viva Turkey for Cats, Viva Pure Turkey, and Viva Beef & Turkey for Puppies. The issue was discovered during an inspection by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) and the North Carolina Department of Agriculture, which found *Listeria monocytogenes* in samples of Viva Turkey for Dogs from the specified lot. Although the products were slated for destruction, some were inadvertently shipped to consumers. The recalled products were distributed nationwide to all 50 states and the District of Columbia between May 16, 2024, and June 28, 2024. As of the announcement, no illnesses had been reported. One source notes the recall was officially initiated on June 12, 2024, and that the products were co-packed by The Lewis Sausage Company, Inc. <9> During its summer session held at the 2024 AVMA Convention in Austin, Texas, the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA) House of Delegates (HOD) sanctioned updates to its Principles of Veterinary Medical Ethics (PVME). The revisions, which were passed during the HOD's meeting on June 20-21, 2024, are intended to make the policy more clear and user-friendly. A key addition is a new Code of Conduct, which establishes standards for providing competent medical care, balancing patient welfare with client needs and public safety, and maintaining professionalism. The overall convention took place from June 21-25, 2024.

Prediction target period: from 2024-10-27 to 2025-01-12. Recent related events (events are separated by numbered tags): <1> A Vetsource white paper, titled “Behavior shift: Implications of today's pet owner trends on veterinary medicine in 2025,” analyzed data through August 2024 from 6,574 U.S. veterinary practices, revealing a notable decline in patient visits. [6, 7] The findings, first presented in October 2024 , show that patient visits decreased by 2.3% year-over-year. [7, 8] Furthermore, the analysis highlighted a significant shift in pet owner behavior, with the average time between appointments increasing to 85.8 days between July 2023 and July 2024, a 48% rise compared to three years prior. [6, 8] These trends are attributed to economic pressures on clients, as veterinary service inflation rose by 8% in the last year, a rate 1.6 times higher than national inflation. [7, 9] The report also noted a 1.9% decrease in the total number of active patients and reduced client spending on items like therapeutic diets and parasiticides. [6, 8] <2> On September 25, 2024, the American Society for the Prevention of Cruelty to Animals (ASPCA) announced a $5 million grant initiative to support animal shelters across the United States facing challenges such as capacity issues and shortages in staffing and veterinary care. Of this total, at least $3 million is available for non-profit and municipal shelters through an application process open until October 18, 2024, with the remaining funds allocated to existing ASPCA partners. The initiative, part of a larger $15 million in grant funding by the ASPCA in 2024, aims to improve positive outcomes for homeless animals, address their psychological health in shelters, and enhance access to veterinary care for pet owners with limited resources. Individual grants through the ASPCA National Shelter Grants Initiative will range from $20,000 to $95,000. <3> In September 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued two distinct 'do not feed' advisories for separate raw pet food brands due to bacterial contamination. The first advisory, issued on September 20, 2024, warned consumers not to feed pets certain lots of Darwin’s Natural Selections raw cat and dog food. [1, 3] An FDA investigation found that five samples of the products tested positive for Salmonella, and a sixth sample tested positive for both Salmonella and Listeria monocytogenes. [2, 4] The affected Darwin's products were specific lots of the Antibiotic & Grain-Free Chicken Recipe for both cats and dogs, sold in frozen 2-pound packages. [1] Three days later, on September 23, 2024, the FDA issued a second advisory for certain lots of ANSWERS pet food. [2] This warning was prompted by three consumer complaints of sick pets and subsequent FDA testing that found Salmonella and/or Listeria monocytogenes in four batches of the company's dog food. [2] <4> In September 2024, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) issued 'do not feed' advisories for specific lots of raw pet food from two companies, Darwin's Natural Selections and Answers Pet Food, due to contamination with Salmonella and Listeria monocytogenes. The first advisory, issued on September 20, 2024, targeted certain lots of Darwin's Natural Selections' raw cat and dog food after five samples tested positive for Salmonella and a sixth for both Salmonella and Listeria. The FDA recommended a recall, but the manufacturer, Arrow Reliance Inc., did not issue one. Subsequently, on September 22, 2024, Lystn, LLC, the parent company of Answers Pet Food, announced a voluntary withdrawal of certain lots of their raw beef and chicken formulas for dogs. This was followed by an official FDA advisory on September 23, 2024, after samples tested positive for Salmonella and/or Listeria monocytogenes, stemming from three consumer complaints of illness in dogs. While the FDA stated the company had not initiated an adequate recall, Answers maintained it had acted voluntarily and disputed the FDA's characterization of the consumer complaints. No confirmed illnesses were associated with the Answers Pet Food lots. <5> On September 19, 2024, Elanco Animal Health announced it had received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for Zenrelia™ (ilunocitinib tablets). [1, 2, 6, 7] This once-daily oral medication is a Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor used to control itching (pruritus) associated with allergic dermatitis and to manage atopic dermatitis in dogs aged 12 months and older. [1, 7] This approval marked Elanco's entry into the estimated $1.7 billion global canine dermatology market. [1, 2, 3] An earlier announcement on June 27, 2024, had stated that the FDA had completed all major technical sections for the treatment, with Elanco anticipating a U.S. launch in the fourth quarter of 2024. The full approval and launch announcement came on September 19, with product orders beginning immediately and shipping to follow in the subsequent days. [1] In a head-to-head study, Zenrelia was found to be at least as effective as the market incumbent, Apoquel®, at the primary endpoint. [1, 4] The FDA's approval notes that the product label includes a boxed warning regarding the risk of fatal vaccine-induced disease and inadequate immune response to vaccines, advising that dogs should be up-to-date on vaccinations before starting the treatment. [5, 7] <6> Elanco Animal Health announced the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has approved Zenrelia™ (ilunocitinib tablets), a once-daily oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor for the control of itching (pruritus) associated with allergic dermatitis and the control of atopic dermatitis in dogs at least 12 months of age. This marks Elanco's entry into the global canine dermatology market. Zenrelia is the second JAK inhibitor approved by the FDA for this indication and will compete with Apoquel. A head-to-head study demonstrated that a single daily dose of Zenrelia is at least as effective as Apoquel. The new medication can be given with or without food. The Zenrelia label includes a boxed warning regarding safety when administered concurrently with vaccines, recommending that dogs be up-to-date on vaccinations before starting treatment. Elanco began taking orders for Zenrelia following the announcement and expects to start shipping within days. <7> Elanco Animal Health Incorporated has received U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) approval for Zenrelia™ (ilunocitinib tablets), its first entry into the canine dermatology market. [1, 2] Zenrelia is a once-daily oral Janus kinase (JAK) inhibitor for the control of pruritus (itching) associated with allergic dermatitis and for the control of atopic dermatitis in dogs aged 12 months or older. [1, 3, 4] The company announced that Zenrelia will be available at a launch list price approximately 20% lower than the current market-leading JAK inhibitor. [6] A head-to-head study conducted for European Union submission, which compared Zenrelia to the market incumbent Apoquel, found that Zenrelia was at least as effective and that 77% of dogs treated with Zenrelia achieved clinical remission of itch compared to 53% of dogs treated with Apoquel. [5] U.S. veterinarians could begin placing orders immediately following the announcement, with shipping expected to commence within days. This diagnostic tool is notable for its cartridge-based system, which utilizes artificial intelligence and cell-focusing technology to provide advanced Complete Blood Count (CBC) analysis for animals, delivering results with the accuracy of a reference laboratory at the point of care. The global launch is scheduled for the Veterinary Meeting & Expo (VMX) in Orlando, Florida, in January 2025, with the first installations in the USA, Canada, Australia, New Zealand, the United Kingdom, and Ireland to follow. <9> The U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) has identified an ongoing, multi-state outbreak of Salmonella infections linked to contact with small pet turtles. [1] According to the CDC's investigation notice, a total of 63 people have been infected with the outbreak strains of Salmonella (Stanley and Poona) across 22 states. [1] Illnesses started on dates ranging from August 20, 2023, to August 12, 2024. [1] Of the 62 people with available information, 28 (45%) have been hospitalized, with no deaths reported. [1] The median age of those infected is 8 years, with children under 5 being significantly affected. [1] Federal law prohibits the sale and distribution of turtles with shells less than 4 inches long as pets, though they continue to be sold through various outlets. [2, 3]

Launched in 2015 with funding from the Pork Checkoff, SHIC's mission is to protect the US swine herd from emerging disease threats. It concludes that current laws and regulations are outdated, resulting in cumbersome requirements and poor communication that hinder U.S. competitiveness in developing new animal drugs and nutritional ingredients. The panel's recommendations, influenced by the 21st Century Cures Act for human medicine, aim to create a more efficient and flexible regulatory process to better serve veterinarians, pet owners, and the food production industry. The panel concluded that existing laws and regulations for animal health and nutrition are outdated and that cumbersome requirements and processes make the U.S. less competitive globally in developing new animal drugs and nutritional products. The report recommends modernizing the federal oversight of animal drugs, food, and biologics to foster innovation and efficiency, suggesting the 21st Century Cures Act as a model for reform.
